extracted.intended_audience: authors (especially self-publishers) and anyone responsible for a book's packaging/brand
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for authors on using cover art, typography, packaging, and public persona to set correct expectations and reach the right audience for a book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cover as advertisement / evoke the correct feel, genre, and audience
rubrics_metrics.description: A cover is not an illustration. A cover is an advertisement. It should evoke the feel of your story, evoke the genre of your story, and evoke who the audience is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on literal scene depiction; instead make promises about tone, genre, and target reader. Anti-pattern: a cover that signals 'mystery' while the content is a thriller — leads to frustrated readers and negative reaction. Example guidance: comic-book covers often illustrate the conflict rather than a literal scene; this is acceptable because it communicates the book's promise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match current shelf language / research prevailing cover trends
rubrics_metrics.description: Step one when positioning your book is to go to where books like yours are shelved and see what the current trend is. Your cover should be in dialogue with the current cover language for your target niche.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid nostalgic mismatches (e.g., using 1970s-style covers because that's what you liked as a teen) if your market expects modern visual cues. Examine bookstores and online catalogs to learn prevailing palettes, illustration/photo usage, and composition conventions for your subcategory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stand out while still fitting genre conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Design choices should help the book stand out on the shelf while still matching the overall vibe of its shelf-mates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contrast, color saturation, and composition to draw attention (e.g., using warm orange tones among predominantly blue middle-grade spines) while retaining genre signifiers (illustration style, hero placement, typography) so readers both notice and correctly identify the book's category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognizability and findability (consistent brand cues)
rubrics_metrics.description: Brand elements need to be recognizable so readers can find and pick your book; poor or confusing packaging can make your book 'invisible' to its audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example anti-pattern: Tropicana redesign that made the product hard to find and caused sales to fall. Ensure key visual cues are clear and consistent across formats and retail contexts so your audience can locate your work quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Packaging beyond the cover — typography and interior design should reinforce promises
rubrics_metrics.description: Packaging (slipcovers, typography, interior design and typesetting) can and should extend the promises made by the cover and reinforce the reading experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use typographic and physical design choices as storytelling devices where appropriate (example: Illuminae's clear slipcover, printed-through elements, and typography that trails like missile trails). Good packaging fulfills the promise set by the cover and can create a 'surprising yet inevitable' experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author name and public persona set expectations — be consistent
rubrics_metrics.description: Your name and public-facing behavior (social media, public appearances) are part of your brand and make promises to readers about tone and conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide which 'faces' you show publicly and maintain consistency during cycles (book release vs lull). Breaking the promise (e.g., abrupt change in tone or behavior) can alienate followers. Example: Howard's Twitter persona that avoids profanity establishes expectations that should be maintained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity and sustainability of author persona
rubrics_metrics.description: Show aspects of yourself rather than inventing and maintaining an entirely fabricated character; sustainability matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dodecahedron metaphor: choose which faces to present publicly rather than trying to perform a full-time persona. Creating an unsustainable character is emotionally exhausting and risks breakdowns that will damage your brand credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicit external feedback to understand perceived brand
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask other people (writing group, family, readers) to describe what they perceive in your work and brand to get an outside 'mirror' on your promises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use feedback to form a pulse on recurring themes readers notice in your work (worldbuilding, emotional stakes, style), and use that to inform whether your cover/marketing is delivering on those expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor and curate social media balance to maintain brand tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Periodically audit your social feeds to check the balance and ensure you're not unintentionally communicating a skewed tone that misrepresents your brand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your recent posts are overly negative or off-brand, adjust content (e.g., share lighter posts) to preserve the image you want to project. Regular review prevents accidental, cumulative shifts in perceived persona.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose the right typeface/text treatment for your author name and title
rubrics_metrics.description: Typeface, text treatment, and hierarchy (serif vs sans, weathered vs crisp, name size vs title size) communicate genre, tone, and author status and should align with the promises your brand makes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiment with fonts and sizing; document why a particular text treatment fits your brand. Consider whether the author name should be prominent (e.g., Brandon Sanderson) or discreet, and how that decision affects reader expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comp titles and descriptive briefs to define cover direction and promises
rubrics_metrics.description: When describing a cover concept, use comp titles/images and concise descriptive language to communicate the image and the promises it should make.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Homework-style approach: write a clear description of the perfect cover (use comp art if helpful), explain what promises it makes to the audience and how it accounts for audience bias. This helps designers and marketers align execution with intended brand signals.
